matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(reef): parked owner reviews own inbound delivery instead of re-rolling the guard (#132420)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(reef): parked owner reviews own inbound delivery instead of re-rolling the guard (#132420)

* fix(reef): parked owner reviews own inbound delivery; keepalive the inbox socket

A pending owner review threw through the inbox pipeline as a connection
failure: the socket tore down, the ~30s reconnect loop re-delivered the
message, and every redelivery re-ran the live guard before consulting the
review store. Any stray stochastic allow delivered the message with the
review still pending, and one transient guard failure terminally rejected
it to the peer (observed live: 554 re-classifications, then delivery with
no owner decision).

The recorded review decision now owns redelivery: classifyWithReview
consults the review store before any guard call, pending parks the entry
un-acked at the relay with the socket up and the durable cursor held,
later entries keep processing, and the reconcile loop re-polls so an
owner decision completes delivery within ~30s (one final post-approval
classification). Transient guard_failure denials park-and-retry instead
of rejecting the peer; sends still fail fast. The inbox socket also gains
the relay's ping/pong keepalive, preventing the silent idle cuts behind
the periodic 1006 reconnects on long-idle links.

* fix(reef): one durable read observation per parked entry

Re-polling a parked entry every reconcile interval appended a read audit
event per attempt (~2,880/day), filling the bounded audit window. The
flow now records one read per park lifecycle and resumes normal
observation once the entry resolves.

* fix(test): avoid shadowing the inbox entry in the parked-read assertion

* fix(test): register second intentional qa-lab suppression in the allowlist

* fix(gateway): authorize spawn-subtree access from durable session lineage

Under tools.sessions.visibility=tree, sessions_history/sessions_send
authorization resolves the target with a spawnedBy selector, and the
exact-key sessions.resolve gate answered it with the child-listing
display filter: run-liveness windows (ended >30m, stale >2h, store-only
30m/1h) and live-controller supersession of the stored spawnedBy field.
Once a child's run ended or was replaced by restart recovery and aged
out of those windows, the parent lost history/send access even though
sessions_list — which reads the durable entry.spawnedBy/parentSessionKey
facts — kept showing the child with its parent linkage.

Exact-key spawnedBy resolution is spawn-lineage ownership, not list
discovery: it now consults the durable direct-child fact owned by
session-child-sessions (entry.spawnedBy/parentSessionKey), falling back
to the live run controller, with no display windows. Discovery selectors
(label/sessionId/shortId) keep list semantics as documented.

Regression tests fail on pre-fix code: unit coverage for expired display
windows and steered controllers, plus a restart-integration test that
drives the real recovery pass and asserts parent history/send tree
authorization survives after the recovered run ends.

matched_commits.full_message:
fix(cron): current-session automations fail with "Channel is required" on webchat-only gateways (#131975)

* fix(cron): complete current-target automations without an external channel route

A sessionTarget=current agentTurn automation on a webchat-only gateway
failed its whole run with 'Channel is required (no configured channels
detected)' even though the completion had already committed durably to
the target conversation. The current-session completion decided whether
an external announce was still owed by string-matching 'webchat' against
the session-key prefix, which misses Control UI dashboard sessions
(agent:<id>:dashboard:<uuid>), and the resulting delivery-target error
was exempt from the #94058 turn-success preservation — a silent failure
on the default path.

Decide external-delivery necessity from the resolution's recorded route
instead: a failed resolution that names no deliverable external channel
has nothing external backing the conversation, so the committed
completion is the delivery and the run succeeds. A failed resolution
that does name an external channel keeps the run successful and records
the failure as the run's delivery error, distinguishing 'turn succeeded,
delivery failed' from 'turn failed'. The delivery preview mirrors the
same rule instead of showing 'will fail-closed' for these jobs.

Live-verified on an isolated no-channel gateway built from this branch:
a one-shot current-target automation bound to a dashboard session ran,
committed its result to the conversation transcript, persisted
status=succeeded, and auto-deleted.

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: feat(docker): install openssh-client in the runtime image (#131710)
matched_commits.full_message:
feat(docker): install openssh-client in the runtime image (#131710)

* feat(docker): install openssh-client in the runtime image

The runtime stage installs `git` but not `openssh-client`, so the published
image has no `ssh` binary.

`src/agents/sandbox/ssh.ts` spawns `ssh` directly, defaulting to the bare
`ssh` command name, so an SSH-backed sandbox session on the published image
fails at start with `spawn ssh ENOENT`. The same gap means `git` cannot use
SSH remotes despite `git` being installed.

`OPENCLAW_IMAGE_APT_PACKAGES` adds the package at build time and is the
supported workaround today, and the prerequisite is documented in
`docs/gateway/openshell.md`. Installing it by default removes the need to
maintain a derived image to use a backend that already ships in the product.

This departs from the opt-in pattern that `OPENCLAW_INSTALL_DOCKER_CLI`
establishes for sandbox backend dependencies. The argument for the departure
is cost: the Docker CLI adds ~50MB plus a third-party apt repository, where
this measures 7.60MB (1452453516 -> 1460057262 bytes, 0.52%) from the base
distribution already in use.

`src/dockerfile.test.ts` asserts the runtime package list as an exact
string, so its three assertions are updated to match. No behavioral test
changes.

Client only. No SSH server, and no change to sandbox defaults or behavior.

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(memory): bound the embedding cache with a built-in default (#131121)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(memory): bound the embedding cache with a built-in default (#131121)

* fix(memory): bound the embedding cache with a built-in default

`memory_embedding_cache` grows without limit. The LRU that this issue asks
for already exists: `pruneEmbeddingCacheIfNeeded` implements it fully. It is
simply unreachable, because `DEFAULT_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES` is `undefined`, so the
`if (!max || max <= 0) return` guard fires on every call.

783a5d21cfc (#111382, "purge numeric tuning knobs behind built-in defaults")
replaced the operator knob with a named default but never chose a value:

  - maxEntries: overrides?.cache?.maxEntries ?? defaults?.cache?.maxEntries,
  + maxEntries: DEFAULT_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES,
  + const DEFAULT_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES = undefined;

Operators could cap the cache before that commit and cannot after it;
`memory.search.cache.maxEntries` is now rejected by config validation
(src/config/dead-config-keys.test.ts:122), so no setting restores it.

Give the default a value, at the config owner, finishing #111382's stated
intent rather than re-adding config surface. 50_000 stays above observed live
chunk counts (25,897 and 38,985 in openclaw/openclaw#114612); a cap below the
working set would evict rows the next sync needs and force paid re-embedding.

Refs: #114612

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(memory): enforce the embedding cache bound on every sync

The default cap only took effect during a full reindex. `pruneEmbeddingCacheIfNeeded`
was called from inside `runInPlaceReindex`'s shadow rebuild, so it bounded the
temporary rebuild database and never the live one. The incremental branches of

and drop the shadow-only call so there is one canonical enforcement point.

Regression test drives `runSync` down the incremental path and asserts the prune
runs; on pre-fix code it observes zero prunes.

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(tool-call-repair): stop re-parsing the whole response per candidate delta (#122513)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(tool-call-repair): stop re-parsing the whole response per candidate delta (#122513)

* fix(tool-call-repair): stop re-parsing the whole response per candidate delta

The streaming tool-call normalizer resolved Markdown protection by materializing
the entire accumulated response and re-parsing it on every candidate-shaped delta,
so a bracket-dense answer cost one full CommonMark parse per line. Work grew
quadratically with response size while emitting byte-identical output.

Carry fenced-code state forward as visible text is appended, and answer protection
from that state when it is provable. The tracker is deliberately conservative: it
models fenced blocks only, marks fence parity permanently unknown when it sees a
delimiter it cannot classify, and returns no answer for inline spans, indented
code, block quotes and lists, so those still take the authoritative full parse.

Measured on the real shared normalizer with the real findCodeRegions resolver:
a 27 KB bracket-dense answer went from 600 full parses / 6055 ms to 0 / 59 ms,
and doubling the response no longer quadruples the re-parsed characters.

Refs #119478

* fix(tool-call-repair): make the fence-only stream fast path opt-in

ClawSweeper flagged the new fence-only fast path (added in this branch to
avoid re-parsing the whole response per candidate delta) as unconditionally
trusted for any caller-supplied resolveProtectedRanges, even though the fast
path only proves fence state. A resolver whose protected ranges are not
fences (e.g. an unfenced caller-defined region) would silently lose its
protection, since the fast path's "not protected" verdict was used directly
without ever consulting the general resolver.

Add PlainTextToolCallStreamNormalizerOptions.protectedRangesFenceCompatible,
an explicit opt-in a caller sets only when its resolver's protected ranges
are exactly the CommonMark fenced/indented/inline code shapes the fast path
models. Without it, the stream always falls back to the authoritative full
parse, matching the resolver's documented (fully generic) contract. Opt the
two current findCodeRegions-backed callers in
(attempt-tool-call-text-promotion.ts, provider-stream-shared.ts), since
findCodeRegions is exactly that shape and the fast path already yields to
the full parse for everything it does not model.

Regression test proves an unfenced, non-fence caller-defined protected range
survives the stream when the fast path is not opted in; reverting the fix
makes it fail with the protected payload silently stripped.

AI-assisted change.

* chore: refresh PR head (keep open for maintainer review)

* fix(tool-call-repair): run the fence-state fast path before resolving cumulative partials

resolvePartialProtectionCheck ran ahead of resolveProtectionFastPath via a
bare `??`, and it fully re-parses the provider's cumulative "partial"
snapshot whenever one validates against the current delta — which
OpenAI-completions and Mistral attach to every text delta. So for exactly
the transport shape this PR targets, the fast path never got a chance to
answer and the quadratic full-response parse persisted despite
protectedRangesFenceCompatible being set.

Reorder so the O(delta) fence-state check runs first; the partial-snapshot
resolver (still a full parse, just of the partial's own text) and the
tracked-context materialize path remain as fallbacks in the same order as
before for callers that don't opt into the fast path, or for deltas the
fast path can't decide from carried state alone.

Added a regression built on the existing bracket-dense-fenced-answer test,
but with a growing cumulative `partial` attached to every delta (the
OpenAI-completions/Mistral shape) — RED on the prior ordering (300 full
parses, one per line), GREEN after the reorder (bounded, same as the
no-partial case).

* fix(tool-call-repair): use a monotonic cursor for fast-path offset lookups

The closure returned by resolveProtectionFastPath rescanned every recorded
line start from index 0 on every offset query. findPotentialCallStart
queries it once per candidate in a single left-to-right scan, so a large
authoritative snapshot with many literal calls made a lookup
Theta(lines x candidates) instead of Theta(lines) -- a ~350KB/16,000-call
snapshot took ~1.5s through the fast path versus ~0.17s through the full
Markdown resolver, undermining the reordering fix.

Offsets are always queried in non-decreasing order (index only advances in
the caller's scan), so a cursor that only moves forward keeps total lookup
work linear across the whole scan.

Added a correctness test for successive increasing-offset queries and a
performance regression built on codex review's own repro shape (20,000
literal calls in one fenced snapshot): RED on the prior linear rescan
(~260ms, comfortably over a 50ms budget), GREEN with the cursor.

* fix(tool-call-repair): stop rescanning the carried partial line on every delta

advanceProtectionScanState searched (partialLine + text).indexOf("\n") on
every call. partialLine never contains a newline by construction, so only
`text` itself can complete a line -- searching the concatenated buffer
re-copies and re-scans the entire carried prefix each time, making a long
newline-free stream (fed in small provider-sized deltas, no candidate or
fence involved) quadratic even though nothing but plain prose is streaming.

Search `text` alone; append to partialLine without touching it when no
newline is found, and only concatenate the carried prefix once, to build
the single line that spans the delta boundary.

Regression: 40,000 x 10-byte deltas (400 KB), matching codex review's own
repro shape -- RED on the prior implementation (~1.2s), GREEN after (well
under the 200ms budget).

* fix(tool-call-repair): advance the fence-state scan when the pending-queue-overcap path replays a false positive

Every other false-positive replay site feeds the replayed text into
advanceProtectionContext so the carried fence-state scan stays in sync with
what was actually streamed. The pendingQueueOverCap branch (a side-channel
event queue growing past MAX_PENDING_EVENTS/MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES while a text
candidate is pending) replayed its false positive but never did, so the
fast path could fall out of sync with reality afterward -- reporting a
later candidate as unprotected because it never saw the fence the replayed
text opened or closed, exactly the failure direction the whole fast path
must never risk.

Mirrors the identical fix already present at the main delta loop's
false-positive branch a few hundred lines above. Full existing suite
(175 tests) stays green; this specific site's exact trigger (queue count
or bytes overflowing while a text candidate straddles a protected range)
needs a materially larger repro to isolate safely.

* fix(tool-call-repair): distrust the fast path when a partial reveals an unstreamed earlier block

The carried fence-state scan only ever advances from text this normalizer
actually streamed as its own delta. When an earlier content block was never
streamed individually -- it only ever appears already-complete inside a
later delta's cumulative `partial` snapshot -- the scan has no idea it
existed, so a candidate in the following block that is genuinely inside a
fence that earlier block opened gets reported as unprotected. The prior
existing test for this exact scenario happened to end its candidate on an
incomplete last line, which independently makes the fast path decline for
an unrelated reason and accidentally masked the bug.

Detect the gap cheaply (a length comparison, not a parse): compare how much
text protectionBlockStart says the scan has tracked against how much text
the partial's own content shows preceding this block. When the partial
knows more, skip the fast path entirely so resolvePartialProtectionCheck
(which reads the partial's own authoritative text, unaffected by what our
own scan tracked) gets to answer instead.

Added a variant of the existing "uses cumulative partials..." test with a
complete final line, isolating the real bug from the incomplete-line
quirk that masked it -- RED before this fix (only the closing fence
survived, the literal tool-call text silently vanished), GREEN after.

* fix(tool-call-repair): treat any preceding-length mismatch as untracked, not just excess

The carried fence-state scan advances in EVENT order; a cumulative
partial's per-block offsets are in CONTENT-INDEX order. These normally
agree, but a provider can stream an active later block before an earlier
one (a supported interleaved-blocks shape) -- then the earlier block's own
content-order offset (0, since it is first in the assembled message) is
LESS than what the scan has tracked (event-order text from the block that
streamed first). The prior ">" check only caught the partial revealing
MORE preceding text than tracked; it missed this direction entirely, so a
genuine unfenced call in the earlier block could still be reported
protected by state that describes an unrelated later block's context.

"!==" catches a mismatch in either direction, not just excess.

Regression: an earlier block streams second, after a later block has
already opened a fence in event order. RED under a ">" check (the real
call gets treated as protected/literal and never recognized); GREEN with
"!==". Verified via the intermediate streamed events specifically, since
the terminal path's own full parse would mask the bug by always
re-deciding correctly regardless of what the streaming fast path picked.

* fix(tool-call-repair): validate prefix identity, not just its length, before trusting the scan

A length match between the event-order-tracked prefix and the partial's
content-order offset does not prove they are the same text. Interleaved
blocks streamed out of content-index order can produce the same aggregate
tracked length from different actual text (e.g. a backtick fence opened in
event order vs a tilde fence opened in content order) -- same length,
opposite fence identity. The prior length-only check missed this, letting
a later block's real fenced call get evaluated against unrelated tracked
state and wrongly treated as unprotected.

Only pay for the real text comparison when lengths already matched and
there is a non-trivial (nonzero) prefix to compare -- the common
single-block case never reaches it (trivial empty-prefix comparison), and
the cost of the rarer multi-block case is bounded by the preceding block's
own size, not by however large the current block's own growing content is.

Regression: block 1 streams "```\n" first, block 0 streams "~~~\n" second
(matching aggregate length, opposite real fence state), then block 2
streams a call still inside the real (content-order) fence. RED with a
length-only check (silently buffers the call and never resolves it, since
nothing in the test flushes the stream further); GREEN once prefix
identity is verified, correctly streaming it as literal protected text.

* fix(tool-call-repair): cache preceding-prefix trust once per block

The same-length content-order safety check materialized and compared a block’s preceding prefix every time a later candidate was considered. Because protectionChunks also contains the current, still-growing block, the full join repeatedly copied unrelated text even though preceding-context trust cannot change within that block, reviving the quadratic work this fast path exists to avoid.

Cache that verdict at the content-block boundary and reset it with the block snapshot. Build only the fixed-size prefix needed by the comparison, stopping once protectionBlockStart characters have been collected.

The new stress fixture initially put the next block’s backticks directly after a 200,000-character newline-free line. Text blocks concatenate without separators, so this was not a CommonMark fence: the conservative scanner correctly entered structuralUnknown and fell back to the authoritative resolver 300 times. Keep the prefix exactly 200,000 characters but terminate its line so the regression exercises the intended valid fence instead of a mid-line delimiter.

Regression: RED as handed off with 300 resolver calls; decline tracing isolated the malformed mid-line fence rather than hasUntrackedPrecedingContext. GREEN with a newline-terminated 200,000-character prefix and 300 cumulative-partial candidate deltas, proving the prefix decision and materialization stay bounded while the protected text streams unchanged.

* fix(tool-call-repair): never cache prefix trust from a candidate with no partial

partial is optional on every event type, so the first candidate in a block
can arrive with none at all. hasUntrackedPrecedingContext correctly has
nothing to compare in that case, but the per-block cache
(protectionBlockPrefixTrusted) treated that "no data" the same as a
confirmed match and locked in "trusted" for the rest of the block. A
later, separate candidate in the same block that DOES carry a partial --
revealing a genuine event-order/content-order mismatch from interleaved
blocks -- then inherited the stale default instead of getting its own
check, letting the wrong (event-order) fence state decide it.

hasUntrackedPrecedingContext now returns undefined for "no data to compare",
distinct from a confirmed true/false; the cache is only written on a
confirmed result, so a block whose first candidate had no partial still
gets a fresh check on its next one. A block that never sees any partial at
all correctly stays trusted throughout (nothing ever contradicts the scan,
so it remains the only source of truth) -- confirmed via the existing
bracket-dense no-partial regression, which caught an earlier draft of this
fix that flipped the wrong default.

Regression: a complete, partial-less call resolves first in a block, then
a second candidate in the same block carries a partial showing the block
actually comes first in content order (opposite fence state from event
order). RED with the cache treating "no data" as "trusted" (the second
candidate is wrongly evaluated against event-order state, gets buffered,
and silently vanishes since nothing resolves it); GREEN once only a
confirmed verdict is cached.

* fix(tool-call-repair): invalidate cached preceding-context trust when an earlier block grows

The per-block cache assumed a block's preceding text never changes across
its own deltas once first observed. That holds when earlier blocks are
already finished, but not when an earlier block is itself still actively
streaming: it can grow between two candidate checks in a later block
without the content index ever switching away and back (which would
otherwise reset the cache via beginProtectionBlock). A boolean-only cache
reused a stale "trusted" verdict from before that growth, letting the
wrong (event-order) fence state decide a later candidate even though a
newer partial already reported the real, changed preceding text.

Replaced the plain boolean cache with a verdict keyed by the preceding
length it was validated against (PrecedingContextVerdict, returned by the
renamed resolvePrecedingContextTrust). A later delta whose partial reports
a different preceding length invalidates the cache and forces a fresh
comparison; a matching length still reuses the cached verdict, keeping the
common (stable) case just as cheap as before.

Regression: block 0 streams "~~~\n" for real; a first, complete call in
block 1 confirms trust against it. A second candidate in block 1 then
arrives with a partial showing block 0 grew to "~~~\n~~~\n" (closing that
fence in content order) -- the earlier verdict must not be reused. RED
with a length-agnostic cache reuse (the real, unfenced second call is
wrongly buffered as protected and never resolves); GREEN once a changed
preceding length forces re-validation.

* test(ollama): prove plain-text tool-call fence protection through the real NDJSON transport (#122513)

Real loopback /api/chat NDJSON server driven through createOllamaStreamFn:
real HTTP, real SSRF-guarded fetch, real NDJSON parsing, real
createPlainTextToolCallCompatWrapper, real Markdown protection. Pins the
safety contract at the transport seam (bracket-dense fenced answer stays
byte-identical, including a complete fenced [read] call, while the same
call outside the fence is normalized away) and pins the raw delta shape
(one text_delta per NDJSON record, no cumulative partial) that the
packages/tool-call-repair bounded-resolution suites replicate.

feat(browser): agent requests/text/emulate + snapshot query, and inline browser-tab thumbnail cards (#131592)

* feat(browser): agent requests, text, and emulate actions plus snapshot query filter

The browser control service already collected network requests and served
device/media/timezone/locale emulation, and Playwright could read page text,
but none of it was exposed to the model. The agent tool now maps them:

- action=requests: bounded network log (filter substring, limit, clear)
- action=text: article/main/body innerText via a new guarded GET /text route;
  hard-capped, no model-provided JS, wrapped as untrusted external content
- action=emulate: device/colorScheme/timezoneId/locale via the existing
  /set/* routes, ordered, with an applied list
- snapshot query=...: token AND-match filter over the formatted snapshot so
  ref discovery no longer needs full-tree reads

Successful tab-scoped results also attach a bounded details.browserTab
{targetId, url, title} descriptor consumed by the Control UI browser-tab
preview card (UI metadata only; replay strips details). Capability gating
drops the Playwright-only actions on Chrome DevTools MCP profiles, and the
tab-bound action list includes the new actions.

* feat(ui): inline browser-tab thumbnail cards in the chat transcript

Browser runs used to render as a text-only 'Used Browser xN' row whose
expanded rows showed raw CDP target ids. The transcript now renders a
browser-tab card - favicon-style globe, page title, URL, and a live
thumbnail of the tab - for each tab an agent touches, live during the run
and in history.

The thumbnail never rides the tool result or the WebSocket: the client
captures it itself over the existing browser.request path (same mechanism
as the browser panel), single-flight per tab with a bounded image cache,
refreshed only when a newer completed result for that tab lands. Cards
collapse to one per tab per turn (latest wins). Clicking a card opens the
browser panel. Without browser.request or after tab close, the card
degrades to a static title/URL chip.

The history projection allowlists the bounded details.browserTab descriptor
(targetId/url/title) that the browser tool now emits; live tool-stream
details already flowed. No new gateway events, no config, no protocol
changes.

* test: register the browser innerText suppression in the lint allowlist

The new browser text action reads rendered visible text via locator
innerText(), which is the semantic point of the action; register the
intentional unicorn/prefer-dom-node-text-content suppression so the
production-suppression allowlist gate stays exact.

* feat(ui): browser card miniature scaling, bottom bar, and tab menu

Review feedback on the browser-tab card: the thumbnail now shows the whole
viewport scaled down (tiny-but-at-scale) instead of a cropped top band, and
the identity moved to a bottom bar - globe, title, URL - with hover-revealed
actions: an Open button into the browser panel and an overflow menu with
Copy URL and Open in new tab. Without a capturable tab the card is the bar
alone.

* fix(ui): route the browser card's external open through openExternalUrlSafe

The boundary guard requires the canonical safe-external-open helper instead
of raw window.open.

* fix(ui): move the browser card menu onto the shared wa-dropdown primitive

The web-awesome ownership guard forbids hand-rolled role=menu popovers and
the cursor policy owns pointer rules; the overflow menu now uses the shared
dropdown (roles, dismissal, and cursor handled by the primitive) with the
new-tab item marked data-new-tab-action.

* style(ui): text-only browser card menu items

* fix(browser/ui): descriptor on emulate/console results; card click selects its tab

ClawSweeper review findings: emulate and tab-scoped console results carry a
targetId but were excluded from the browserTab descriptor wrapper, so their
successful results could not render the browser-tab card; and the card's
panel-toggle event carried only open:true, leaving a different active tab in
place. The wrapper now covers both actions, the toggle contract gains an
optional targetId, and the panel selects that tab on targeted open requests
(embedded and docked paths).

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: feat(comfy): support custom headers and per-request seed randomization (#130098)
matched_commits.full_message:
feat(comfy): support custom headers and per-request seed randomization (#130098)

* feat(comfy): support custom headers and per-request seed randomization

Local-mode ComfyUI requests only ever sent Content-Type, so a local
instance reachable behind HTTP auth (Basic auth, a bearer token) had no
way to authenticate. Add a generic headers config key, merged over the
plugin's own headers -- same shape as the ollama plugin's established
remote.headers pattern, rather than inventing a comfy-specific scheme.

Also add optional seedNodeId/seedInputName: without it, a static
workflow file's sampler seed never changes between submissions, so
every generation was silently identical whenever the operator's
workflow relies on a fresh random seed per run.

* fix(comfy): resolve headers through the SecretInput path, not plaintext-only

The new headers config accepted only literal strings, so a credential-bearing
value (Authorization for a gated ComfyUI instance) had no path to secret
storage -- unlike the existing apiKey field, which already resolves through
resolveSecretInputString with an env-backed fallback. Mirrors that same
pattern per-header, plus the ollama plugin's established header-secret
precedent: a header pointed at a SecretRef that can't be resolved fails the
request outright instead of silently sending it unauthenticated.

* fix(comfy): resolve non-env header SecretRefs, hide capability on unresolvable ones

resolveComfyHeadersConfig only ever resolved env-sourced SecretRefs (a
manual process.env fallback bolted onto inspect-mode); any file,
keychain, or plugin-backed reference always threw, despite the schema
and docs advertising the same SecretRef shape apiKey accepts. Now
resolves through resolveConfiguredSecretInputString (the same async
resolver the ollama plugin's own headers use) for the non-literal case,
so a real non-env credential provider actually works.

Separately, isComfyCapabilityConfigured returned true for local mode
without ever inspecting headers, so an unavailable Authorization
SecretRef advertised an image/video/music tool that would always throw
on invocation. Extends the same sync inspect-based veto
resolveComfyApiKey already applies for cloud mode's apiKey.

hasUnavailableComfyHeaderSecret treated any non-env SecretRef as

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(ai): carry the Responses system prompt via instructions, not input[0] (#130206)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(ai): carry the Responses system prompt via instructions, not input[0] (#130206)

* fix(ai): carry the Responses system prompt via instructions, not input[0]

Every non-Codex OpenAI Responses request embedded the system prompt as
input[0]. HTTP continuation compares input byte-for-byte against the
cached previous request to decide whether it can reuse
previous_response_id, and the embedded runner rebuilds the system
prompt fresh every attempt from live runtime state (active background
processes, watched sessions, active-memory context) -- so ordinary
state churn between two turns permanently defeated continuation.
Native Codex/ChatGPT already avoided this by sending the system prompt
via the separate instructions field; broaden that to every Responses
request (instructions was previously Codex-only) and exclude
instructions from the continuation comparator, matching how input is
already excluded there.

xAI's /responses/compact endpoint has no instructions field (system
prompt must be the first input message, confirmed against
docs.x.ai/developers/advanced-api-usage/context-compaction) and was
about to silently lose the system prompt on every compaction request
once it stopped riding along in input. Re-embed it just for that
request body via a new buildOpenAIResponsesCompactSystemMessage
helper, with its own regression coverage for the developer/system role
selection since that invariant no longer has any other test path.

* fix(ai): gate the Responses instructions field behind compat.supportsInstructions

A proxy-compatible Responses endpoint that silently ignores `instructions`
(confirmed for at least xAI's compact endpoint, plausible for other
custom/proxy routes with no established contract) would drop the system
prompt with no error -- the request still returns 200. Add a
compat.supportsInstructions escape hatch, defaulting to on, mirroring
the existing supportsStore/supportsPromptCacheKey pattern: when an
operator sets it false, the system prompt goes back to being embedded
in `input[0]` (the pre-instructions behavior) instead of `instructions`.

Addresses the maintainer review finding on #130206.

* fix(ai): expose supportsInstructions through config and catalog contracts

usesInstructionsField already read compat.supportsInstructions at
request-build time, but strict config and catalog normalization dropped
the key, so no configured model could actually set it. A proxy that
silently ignores top-level instructions had no supported way to opt out.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Vk2cBRQdErwRtPea8VuhG6

* fix(ai): default the Responses instructions field off for unverified proxy routes

usesInstructionsField defaulted true for any api:"openai-responses" model
regardless of endpoint, including arbitrary custom/local proxies OpenClaw
has no bundled knowledge of. HTTP continuation only ever engages on the
exact native api.openai.com route, so an unverified proxy got nothing in
return for the risk of silently losing its system prompt if it doesn't
honor `instructions`. Default now follows the same known-endpoint
classification the file already uses for reasoning/input-status payload
shaping; xAI's already-verified main route is unaffected since it's a
named endpoint class, not "custom"/"local".

Also updates the one stale test this flips (xAI compact-endpoint replay
no longer embeds the system prompt in input[0], matching what the
original PR's instructions-field change already does for that route) and
documents supportsInstructions in the custom-provider compat table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Vk2cBRQdErwRtPea8VuhG6

* fix(ai): narrow the instructions-field default to only confirmed-verified routes

usesVerifiedInstructionsEndpoint (formerly usesUnverifiedProxyEndpoint's
inverse) treated every named endpointClass except custom/local as
verified -- but recognizing a hostname (for SSRF/base-URL matching) is
not the same as having confirmed that host's Responses API honors
`instructions`. Bundled classes like OpenCode and GitHub Copilot have no
such confirmation, so their existing users could silently lose their
system prompt on upgrade. Narrowed the default-on set to exactly the two
routes actually verified: native OpenAI (definitionally) and xAI's main
route (confirmed by direct testing, per the existing compact-endpoint
carve-out). Every other route, named or not, now defaults to the
pre-existing input-embedded behavior unless compat.supportsInstructions
opts it in explicitly.

Also lands a permanent committed integration test
(openai-responses-payload-policy.instructions.integration.test.ts) over
a real loopback HTTP+SSE server -- no SDK mocking -- asserting the
literal wire request for both the unverified-default-off and
explicit-opt-in cases, following the same pattern as
openai-responses-client.continuation.integration.test.ts.

The comparator already strips instructions before comparing requests

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(ai): add gated live proof for the instructions default + continuation

Committed, rerunnable proof of the actual open question -- does a real
native OpenAI Responses request carry the system prompt via top-level
instructions, and does HTTP continuation still correctly reuse
previous_response_id once the prompt moved out of input. Follows the
established openai-responses-client.continuation.live.test.ts pattern
(gated on OPENCLAW_LIVE_TEST=1 + OPENAI_API_KEY, skipped otherwise).

Captures the literal request bytes via a globalThis.fetch wrapper
rather than a forward-proxy: proxying would require overriding the
model's baseUrl to a loopback address, which would itself defeat the
native-route classification under test (the continuation eligibility
check in openai-responses-websocket.ts requires an exact
https://api.openai.com/v1 origin/path match and treats any other
baseUrl, including a proxy's loopback address, as non-native).

Uses the same secret-recall semantic proof as the reference continuation
live test: turn 2 can only produce the secret given in turn 1 if the
real API actually resolved server-side state through
previous_response_id, since the trimmed turn-2 request never repeats it
-- structural proof (previous_response_id present) alone can't rule out
a silent full-history fallback producing the same visible answer.

Verified: run against the real API twice (once before, once after an
unrelated lint fix) -- both passed, confirming turn 1 carries
instructions with no previous_response_id, turn 2 carries
previous_response_id plus the correctly-recalled secret with a
single-message trimmed input.

fix(codex): turns using dotted MCP tool names end muted with no reply (#128900)

Codex records native MCP and connector calls under dotted namespaced ids
("codex_apps.slack.slack_send"). The settled-turn projection validated
recorded names against the function-tool registration charset, so any
settled turn that used such a tool failed isolated finalization with
"found an invalid tool name", the plugin-harness error has no embedded
fallback, and the run ended errored+mute with nothing posted to the
channel.

Dotted names are legal where projected names actually go: Codex
thread/inject_items deserializes ResponseItem::FunctionCall { name:
String } (codex-rs app-server/src/request_processors/turn_processor.rs,
protocol/src/models.rs), and the Responses API round-trips them
in-thread. Admit "." in TOOL_NAME_PATTERN and name the offending tool in
the rejection error so remaining charset gaps are diagnosable from logs.

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(agents): continue settled tool batches after a transport drop (#130721)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(agents): continue settled tool batches after a transport drop (#130721)

* fix(agents): continue settled tool batches after a transport drop

A transient provider transport failure (WebSocket drop, socket reset) that
lands after every tool call in the batch has settled used to kill the turn:
any executed side-effecting tool marks the attempt replay-unsafe, and every
recovery path is gated on replay safety, so the runner surfaced the generic
"Agent couldn't generate a response" warning even though the tool results
were already persisted and nothing needed to be re-run. Under code mode every
tool call is exec, so any turn with a tool call died on a socket hiccup.

Continue such attempts from the persisted transcript with the existing
mid-turn continuation prompt, bounded to two continuations per run and only
for silent errored turns with transient evidence; prompt resubmission, profile
rotation, and model fallback stay closed for side-effecting attempts.

* fix(agents): narrow settled transport recovery

Require provider transport diagnostics before continuing a replay-unsafe settled tool batch, leaving rate-limit failures with the existing failover owner. Preserve the prior last-call usage only when a compaction retry fails before recording a replacement, without overwriting a newer successful call after later processing errors.

* fix(agents): restore retry usage only on failure

Keep the previous exact usage hidden while a compaction retry is active. Restore it only when the retry terminates with an error before recording a new call; a successful replacement call remains authoritative across later processing failures.

* fix(agents): require settled tools for transport resume

Keep the parked Code Mode exception scoped to overflow recovery. Provider transport recovery now requires every tool lifecycle item to be settled, with regression coverage for a suspended nested Code Mode run.

* fix(agents): fence suspended code mode recovery

Reject transcript continuation whenever the settled batch still carries producer-recorded suspended Code Mode work, even if the outer lifecycle count has reached zero. Cover that exact state in the recovery regression.

* fix(agents): resume parked code mode after transport drop

Use the canonical mid-turn settled evidence for transport continuation so producer-recorded parked Code Mode runs can resume from the current transcript. This lets the model call wait for the existing cell without replaying the original prompt or exec.

Cover parked active-count states and preserve the terminal, abort, timeout, visible-output, diagnostic, rate-limit, retry-budget, and no-fallback gates.

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(gateway): keep node-policy approval requester eligible as reviewer (#130967)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(gateway): keep node-policy approval requester eligible as reviewer (#130967)

A turn-driven plugin approval (e.g. Codex exec-server launch) carried the
operator connection that submitted the turn as its requester, and delivery
excluded that connection from the reviewer set. With a single connected
Control UI client the only eligible reviewer was excluded, so the approval
was auto-denied as no-route before anyone could see it.

Node-invoke policy approvals are minted gateway-side and never presented
through the requesting client's RPC response, so the carried connection is
provenance, not a presenter to dedupe: stop excluding it. RPC-ingress
approval paths keep their requester exclusion.

Also extracts the shared plugin-policy test harness into
node-invoke-plugin-policy.test-helpers.ts (the test file crossed the
max-lines lint cap).

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(cli): resolve alias targets from the write snapshot (#128223)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(cli): resolve alias targets from the write snapshot (#128223)

* fix(cli): models aliases add targets a stale model when the alias is remapped concurrently

`openclaw models aliases add <alias> <model-or-alias>` resolved its
`<model-or-alias>` argument from the config loaded at command start, then
entered `updateConfig`, which takes a fresh snapshot and fences the write
on that snapshot's hash. When another writer remapped the source alias in
between, the hash check still passed and the new alias was attached to the
model the argument no longer denoted, and the success line reported that
stale target.

Resolve the argument inside the fenced mutator from the same snapshot that
guards the write, using the resolver `models set` already uses (authored
source aliases first, runtime-materialized built-in aliases second), and
drop the pre-CAS read. This also aligns `aliases add` with `models set`
when an authored alias shares a name with a built-in one.

Closes #127618

* fix(compaction): show the summarizer the audited latest ask

The safeguard reads the latest user ask from the pre-partition window but
only feeds the summarizer the partitioned messages. When recentTurnsPreserve
keeps the ask verbatim and the preserved suffix is head-truncated, the
producer can never reflect it, so every attempt fails
latest_user_ask_not_reflected and compaction cancels, leaving the session
stuck at the context limit.

Hand the bounded ask to the summarizer as untrusted data on every attempt so
the guard only demands what the producer was shown.

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(agents): strip external-content nonce so loop detection blocks repeated wrapped failures (#130261)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(agents): strip external-content nonce so loop detection blocks repeated wrapped failures (#130261)

* fix(agents): strip external-content nonce before loop-detection resultHash

External-content wrappers carry a fresh anti-forgery nonce per result
(createExternalContentMarkerId). The loop detector hashed the wrapper text
including the nonce, so identical failing wrapped tool calls never reached
the no-progress block threshold — the detector warned but never blocked,
leaving the agent to loop until it gave up (#130210).

Strip the wrapper nonce before hashing in extractTextContent, mirroring
the existing stripVolatileSendIds treatment of per-call send ids (#89090).
Only the hash is normalized; the delivered wrapper keeps its nonce, so
anti-forgery is unaffected.

Closes #130210

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(discord): a failing slash command leaves the user watching a spinner that never resolves (#128630)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(discord): a failing slash command leaves the user watching a spinner that never resolves (#128630)

* fix(discord): surface interaction handler failures instead of leaving a spinner

A command handler that threw after deferring left Discord showing a
spinner forever; the failure only reached the Gateway log.

Dispatch now reports a best-effort failure notice before rethrowing, but
only where a spinner is known to exist: responseState 'deferred' with no
follow-up already sent. 'deferred-update' is excluded because the
interaction's original response is the message a component is attached
to, and editing it would overwrite content the user is reading.
'unacknowledged' is excluded because a second initial callback risks
'already acknowledged' and Discord shows its own notice. 'replied' is
excluded because nextReplyAction() would turn the notice into a
contradictory follow-up.

The notice sets allowed_mentions.parse to empty so an exception message
containing @everyone cannot ping the channel.

* fix(discord): report a generic notice instead of the handler exception text

An interaction response is visible to the whole channel, and handler
exceptions routinely carry absolute paths, config keys, and provider
responses. Send fixed text and leave the detail in the Gateway log, which
also removes the mention-injection source rather than only escaping it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(discord): re-check follow-up delivery inside the response queue

hasSentFollowUp is only set once the follow-up REST call resolves, so a
follow-up still in flight when the handler throws left the reporter
deciding against state that was about to change. Move the guard into a
queued operation that re-reads both the response state and follow-up
delivery, so any in-flight follow-up settles and records itself first.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

An unauthorized sender's inline directives are cleared to plain text before

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(github-copilot): allow xhigh and max thinking levels on claude-opus-5 (#129690)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(github-copilot): allow xhigh and max thinking levels on claude-opus-5 (#129690)

* fix(github-copilot): allow xhigh and max thinking levels on claude-opus-5

Copilot users could not select thinking levels above `high` on
`claude-opus-5`. Both `/think xhigh` and `/think max` were rejected and the
picker offered only up to `high`, even with `thinkingDefault: "max"` set.

The bundled manifest entry declared no `supportedReasoningEfforts`, so
`resolveCopilotThinkingLevelMap()` in extensions/github-copilot/models.ts
returned undefined and `clampThinkingLevel()` filtered both tiers out.

A user-side `models.providers` overlay cannot fix this: models.ts
short-circuits `resolveCopilotForwardCompatModel()` when the model is
already in the bundled registry, so the only path that applies a
`thinkingLevelMap` is never reached. The native Claude fallback does not
apply either, since model-utils.ts only consults it for
`api === "anthropic-messages"` routes and Copilot resolves through its
OpenAI-compatible transport.

Declares the effort list the same way extensions/opencode already does for
the same model id. Verified on a live account: after this change `xhigh`
and `max` are selectable and accepted at runtime.

* test(github-copilot): cover Opus 5 manifest reasoning levels

matched_commits.full_message:
fix(read): drop image payload for non-vision models (#127112)

* fix(read): drop image payload for non-vision models

The read tool emitted an omission note for non-vision models ("Current
model does not support images. The image will be omitted from this
request.") but still appended the full base64 image to the response
content, contradicting the note and pushing potentially hundreds of
thousands of tokens a non-vision model cannot use — enough to exhaust
the context window and kill the session on a single image read (#127009).

Drop the image payload in the non-vision branch so the note is true;
keep it for vision-capable and model-unknown cases, matching existing
behavior and tests.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(read): carry vision capability into core read construction

The non-vision image drop only fired when the read tool received a
per-call extension model context. The bare `createReadTool` wrapper the
embedded runtime uses supplies no ctxFactory, so ctx.model was always
undefined there and `getNonVisionImageNote` returned undefined — a
text-only embedded run still attached the full base64 image, exhausting
context with tokens the model cannot use.

Thread the prepared `modelHasVision` boolean — already known at tool
construction from the model's input capability — from
`attempt-tool-prepare` -> `createOpenClawCodingTools` ->
`createCoreCodingTools` -> `createSandboxedReadTool`/`createReadTool` ->
`ReadToolOptions`. `getNonVisionImageNote` now takes the flag as the
primary signal (false drops, true keeps) and falls back to the per-call
context model only when the flag is unknown, preserving the extension
path.

Adds embedded-path regression coverage: the bare `createReadTool`
constructed with `modelHasVision: false` (no per-call ctx) now drops the
image and keeps the note — pre-fix this path attached it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(agents): quiet model turns are aborted by a false "no response from model" idle timeout (#117884)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(agents): quiet model turns are aborted by a false "no response from model" idle timeout (#117884)

* fix(agents): quiet model turns are aborted by a false "no response from model" idle timeout

The embedded runner merges the caller's request signal with the run's
cancellation signal through AbortSignal.any, which produces a new signal
object. The LLM request-activity registry is keyed by signal identity, so
transports that report progress with notifyLlmRequestActivity(options.signal)
now notify the composite while the idle watchdog is still listening on the
signal it handed in. Every keep-alive is dropped, and turns whose only sign of
life is that keep-alive (hidden reasoning on openai-completions, buffered
Claude refusals) are aborted as idle while the model is still responding.

Bridge activity from the composite back to the caller signal at mergeRunSignal,
the single site that holds both, restoring the pre-merge identity for the
activity channel while keeping both cancellation owners. The bridge is disposed
from the caller signal rather than the composite: Node keeps composite signals
that carry an abort listener in a process-wide strong set until the last
listener is removed.

* fix(agents): stop idle activity after run cancellation

* style: satisfy oxfmt import ordering in stream-resolution.test.ts

* fix(agents): release completed watchdog activity bridges

* test(agents): isolate provider stream activity regressions

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(browser): don't steal focus on headed screenshot captures (#105393)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(browser): don't steal focus on headed screenshot captures (#105393)

* fix(browser): don't steal focus on headed screenshot captures

captureScreenshot unconditionally sent Page.bringToFront before every
capture to avoid a headless-specific stall (#100857), but on a headed
browser that activates the visible tab on every screenshot — the
highest-frequency agent operation — repeatedly stealing focus from a
watching user (#105357).

Detect headed-ness via Browser.getVersion userAgent and only skip
activation when the browser is confirmed headed. Headless browsers, and
any case where detection is unavailable, keep activating so the #100857
stall fix is never reintroduced.

Fixes #105357

* fix(browser): trust managed launch flag for screenshot tab activation

The v1 headed-detection sniffed the browser user-agent to decide whether
to activate the tab before a screenshot. A managed headless Chrome can be
launched with a custom --user-agent via extraArgs, which the sniff would
misclassify as headed and drop the activation that prevents the
background-capture stall (#100857).

For a managed browser the profile already holds the authoritative headless
launch flag, so pass it through and let it win over UA sniffing. Attached/
external sessions (headless unknown) keep the best-effort UA fallback. This
also skips the per-screenshot Browser.getVersion round-trip on the common
managed path.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(browser): drop unreliable UA sniff; activate unless confirmed-headed

The re-review flagged a symmetric availability risk in the attached-session
fallback: an attached headless Chrome launched with a custom non-"headless"
--user-agent is misclassified by the UA sniff as headed, suppressing the
activation that prevents the #100857 background-capture stall.

Verified against real Chrome that no runtime signal survives a spoofed UA:
--headless=new with --user-agent=<normal> reports product "Chrome/…", the
spoofed userAgent, and navigator.webdriver === false — indistinguishable from
a headed browser. So the UA sniff cannot be made robust for attached sessions.

Focus-hygiene is only safe where the headless state is authoritative (managed
profiles, via the launch flag). Skip activation ONLY for a confirmed-headed
managed profile; managed headless and every attached/external session keep
activating, so the stall (a hard timeout — strictly worse than an unnecessary
activation) is never risked. This drops the UA sniff and the per-screenshot
Browser.getVersion round-trip entirely. Attached behavior matches current main
(always activate); only managed headed profiles — the primary #105357 case —
change.

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(buzz): messages sent during Gateway downtime are dropped after restart (#117259)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(buzz): messages sent during Gateway downtime are dropped after restart (#117259)

* fix(buzz): messages sent during Gateway downtime are dropped after restart

Every new Gateway process subscribed to Buzz rooms starting at its own
start time, because the lookback flag that enables backlog paging is
process-local. That cutoff is applied as the NIP-01 since filter, so any
room message a human sent while the process was down was never returned
by the relay and never reached the agent or the transcript.

The account gateway now persists a per-account recovery watermark in the
plugin state store. First-ever setup still starts from the current time;
later process starts resume from the saved watermark, clamped to the
existing 24 hour retention floor. The watermark advances only after
inbound handling completes and is stored at the admitted message
created_at, so the inclusive since boundary re-offers the last admitted
message to the existing persistent event-id dedupe guard.

* fix(buzz): keep the cold-start recovery cursor behind unfinished work

Codex review found two ways the recovery watermark could still drop room
messages. Backlog replay dispatches up to eight handlers concurrently, so
a newer message finishing before an older one committed the newer
timestamp; a crash then left the older message with no dedupe record and
a cursor already past it. The stored timestamp was also the sender
controlled created_at, so a future dated room event pushed the cursor
past locally observed time and excluded real downtime messages on the
next start.

The account gateway now tracks a recovery frontier per session. A
checkpoint is the highest completed message time bounded by the oldest
still running message, the oldest failed message, and the receipt time
observed when the message was admitted. Checkpointing stays closed until
the bus reports the room backlog fully drained, so a session that is
still paging history cannot commit past events it has not seen yet.
catchUpHistory now reports drained or incomplete for that signal.

* fix(buzz): scope cold-start recovery per room and fence it at enqueue

Admit replay work into the recovery frontier when it enters the dispatch queue instead of when a worker starts it, so a crash cannot persist a cutoff past an event that is still queued.

Key recovery cursors by room instead of by account, so a room configured after the first start resolves to the current time and gets no backfill, while existing rooms resume from their own cursor.

Record an account-level start marker so the first start under a watermark-aware build recovers the existing retention window instead of repeating the reported loss on the first restart after an upgrade.

* fix(buzz): keep cold-start recovery to accounts that already ran

An account with no persisted cursor is a fresh install as often as it is a
pre-watermark upgrade, and stored state cannot tell them apart, so the first
start no longer replays the retention window. It records the current time as
each room cursor and recovers only from the second start onward.

Dropping the account start marker also removes the interrupted-bootstrap
window where a marker written before the room cursors made the next start
treat cursor-less rooms as initialized.

Recovery state capacity is now derived from the supported room limit instead
of a smaller fixed number, and any non-complete history paging outcome, not
just timestamp-over-limit, holds the recovery frontier undrained.

* fix(buzz): bound the recovery cursor store to each account

ClawSweeper found that the recovery watermark opened one fixed plugin-state
namespace for every account while sizing it at the per-account supported room
count. Plugin-state capacity is enforced per plugin and namespace, so once one
account registered its full room allowance, a second account's register call
threw and its rooms stayed at the current-time cutoff, which is the same
dropped-message outcome this PR set out to fix.

The store is now opened against a namespace derived from the account identity,
so each account carries its own supported room capacity. The account moves out
of the entry key into the namespace, which leaves one account-scoped store path
rather than a fallback, and makes cross-account cursor mixing unrepresentable.

* fix(buzz): simplify durable restart recovery

matched_commits.full_message:
fix(control-ui): chat Markdown preview renders RTL documents left-to-right (#129129)

* fix(control-ui): render the chat Markdown preview in its own text direction

The chat transcript already picks a direction per message
(`chat-message-markdown.ts` sets `dir` from `detectTextDirection`), but the
Markdown preview in the chat detail panel never did. A Hebrew or Arabic
document opened there rendered left-to-right: bullets and quote bars on the
wrong side, table columns in the wrong order, and sentence-final punctuation
detached from its sentence.

Detect the direction from the document source and set `dir` on the reader, then
let the shared `.sidebar-markdown` rules mirror with it by using logical
properties instead of left/right ones. Code blocks get `unicode-bidi: plaintext`
so each hard-wrapped line keeps its own direction — that also covers the raw-text
view, which renders the whole document as one fenced block. Block art carries no
strong characters, so it stays left-to-right as before.

Under LTR the logical properties resolve to exactly the previous physical ones,
so nothing changes for existing documents.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-ui): make the task-list checkbox gap direction-aware

The sidebar sheet moved its indents, quote bar and cell alignment to logical
properties, but `.task-list-item-checkbox` kept `margin-right`. In an RTL
document the label sits to the left of the box, so the physical margin pushed
the gap to the outer edge of the row instead of between the box and its label
— the one remaining place in this sheet where direction still leaked through.

`margin-inline-end` is what the message renderer already uses for the same
control (`chat/text.css` positions it with `inset-inline-start`), so this also
lines the two sheets up.

The RTL and LTR browser tests each grow a task item and assert the computed
margin lands on the inline-end side, mirroring the existing quote-bar and
list-indent assertions.

Formatting proof (node_modules absent in this checkout, so the pre-commit
oxfmt hook could not run): oxfmt 0.60.0 --check and oxlint 1.78.0 both pass
on the changed test file.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(control-ui): assert the checkbox gap by side, not against zero

The assertions added in the previous commit demanded the opposite margin be
0, and `checks-ui` failed on exactly that: 3px in RTL, 4px in LTR. Those are
the UA sheet's own `margin: 3px 3px 3px 4px` on an `input[type=checkbox]`.
The rule overrides only the inline-end side, so the opposite side keeps the
default and never reaches zero.

Assert instead that the sheet's 0.4em resolved onto the expected physical
side — margin-left under RTL, margin-right under LTR — which is the mapping
the fix is actually about and owes nothing to UA defaults.

Verified against a real Chromium before pushing: with `margin-inline-end`
both directions land 5.33px (0.4em of the 13.333px UA control font) on the
inline-end side; with the pre-fix `margin-right` the RTL assertion fails and
the LTR one passes, which is the regression shape this test exists to catch.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* ui(chat): scope the code-block bidi rule to the markdown reader

`unicode-bidi: plaintext` sat in the shared `.sidebar-markdown pre` rule, which
also matches the skills, session-progress-card and agent status-file previews.
Those surfaces never opt into a document direction, so this branch was changing
their code-block rendering while declaring them unchanged.

Move the declaration to `.sidebar-markdown-reader pre` — the chat preview is the
only consumer that sets `dir`. The shared layout properties stay shared, and the
existing direction test already queried the reader-scoped selector, so it is
unaffected. Adds a regression test pinning that a bare `.sidebar-markdown`
surface keeps its previous code-block rendering.

matched_commits.full_message:
fix(gateway): stop persisting passive chat greetings into the durable logbook (#129506)

Every fresh system-agent chat session persisted its generated welcome into
the durable logbook, and the next session seeded that tail back as
history. On a zero-history profile the embedded Control UI custodian
(which loads openclaw.chat.history separately) rendered the identical
'Inference is ready' greeting twice — live plus under an EARLIER divider —
and greetings accumulated on every reconnect.

Persist a newly generated welcome only when the request carries genuine
user input, or when a caretaker welcome delivers a one-shot external-edit
alert (facts.recentExternalEdit) whose audit cursor advances on delivery
and therefore must stay recoverable. Ordinary caretaker, onboarding, and
new-agent welcome-only connections keep the greeting in live engine
context without creating durable transcript rows. Reset boundaries and
real conversation persistence are unchanged.

Regression tests fail pre-fix for all three greeting variants: two
consecutive welcome-only connects must not replay the prior greeting.

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(skills): fork the foreground session for lean experience review (#129282)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(skills): fork the foreground session for lean experience review (#129282)

## What Problem This Solves

Skill Workshop experience review ran as an isolated agent with a re-rendered 60k-character transcript, its own bootstrap, and a trimmed tool surface. Every review was a cold request: no prompt-cache reuse, a large re-serialized trajectory, and a reasoning/tool profile that differed from the foreground turn. Autonomous updates could target any workspace skill, size limits allowed 40 KB skills to grow unchecked (one deployed workspace hit a 21 KB `SKILL.md`), the collection reviewer had to re-list every skill in its plan and read them under a fixed 24k-character budget (a 16-skill workspace failed every pass with "Read every current skill before reconciling"), collection review only recorded successes so a failing pass retried on every Gateway restart, and `openclaw skills curator status` showed nothing about what the last reviews did.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Warm fork.** Experience review now continues the finished turn from the same in-memory session prefix (same session identity, bootstrap, skills prompt, tool schemas, `promptCacheKey`), appends one short review message, and runs with `sessionPersistence: "detached"` so nothing it writes reaches the foreground transcript or session record. Only `skill_workshop` executes; every other tool keeps its schema for cache parity and fails with a next-step message. The gate wraps the core tool list before Code Mode / Tool Search compaction, so catalog-hidden tools stay gated while `tool_call`/`exec` remain callable. `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.skills-policy.test.ts` asserts identical system-prompt and tool digests between a foreground turn and its review, and that `tool_call` reaches `skill_workshop` but not `read` during review. Code Mode swarm globals (`phase`, `log`, `agents.run`) are the `sessions_spawn` capability and gate on the same allowlist, so a review cannot emit foreground lifecycle events or launch collectors. The review shares the foreground session, so it no longer retires that session's MCP runtime on run end; it reuses the warm runtime like any turn. Accepted tradeoff: the review inherits foreground tool construction (it creates the session MCP runtime only when the session has none, and spawns per-attempt LSP servers only when configured), because splitting tool construction from the foreground turn would break the cache-parity invariant this PR exists for.
- **One apply owner, rechecked at the write boundary.** `src/skills/workshop/autonomous-apply.ts` decides apply-vs-pending for both the post-review loop and foreground repair: creates and updates to Workshop-authored skills apply; updates to user-authored skills stay pending with a recorded reason. `applySkillProposalTransition` rechecks path-based ownership under the commit lock for non-operator actors (agent, or no actor), so a claim released after the pre-check cannot let an agent write a user-authored skill; gateway and CLI operators still approve any pending proposal. The user-authored pending write runs under the same commit lock and rereads the row, so an operator apply that lands first is kept. The old `auto-apply.ts` path and name-based `listWorkshopAuthoredSkillNames` are deleted.
- **Sparse collection plan and model-relative reads.** The collection reviewer returns only `write` and `drop` entries; unlisted skills stay untouched, so a 16-skill workspace no longer has to restate 16 keeps. The skill read budget is derived from the model's context window (35%) instead of a fixed 24k characters, with the 10,000-character skill cap still enforced per skill. No windowed read parameters: a skill is read whole or not at all.
- **Weekly cadence.** Collection review runs once every 7 days instead of daily (`REVIEW_INTERVAL_MS`), matching how slowly a skill library actually changes; the attempt is recorded before the model starts, so a failed pass does not retry on every restart.
- **Lean cap.** `AUTONOMOUS_SKILL_MAX_CHARS = 10,000` in `src/skills/workshop/collection-contracts.ts` is enforced by the tool and by collection reconcile; an oversized skill may only shrink. Tool description, experience prompt, and collection prompt were rewritten around procedures-not-records, one trigger per branch, and "NOTHING_TO_LEARN is the correct answer for most turns".
- **Detached runs end quietly.** A detached run writes no transcript or session record and runs under the foreground session key, so `attempt-finalize` now skips agent_end side effects for it: plugins do not observe the review as a foreground turn, and a deep review cannot schedule a successor review of itself.
- **Recorded outcomes.** Experience review records `applied | proposed | nothing | failed` with usage; one attempt per turn, drop on error. `openclaw skills curator status` prints the last collection and experience review outcome.

## User Impact

- Default `auto` mode: experience review reuses the foreground prompt cache and skips message/other tool execution, so review cost is one bounded continuation instead of a cold re-render.
- Autonomous edits touch only Workshop-authored skills; handwritten skills surface as pending proposals for operator approval.
- Autonomous `SKILL.md` results stay ≤ 10,000 characters.
- Collection review runs weekly and succeeds on larger skill libraries. A workspace with no recorded attempt reviews at the first daily check after Gateway start; an upgraded install keeps its recorded last attempt and reviews once it is older than 7 days. The 10,000-character cap applies to the next autonomous write; existing oversized skills are only ever shrunk.
- `openclaw skills curator status` shows the last collection and experience review outcome, time, and tokens.
- Docs: https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/self-learning, https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/skill-workshop

Related: #123866, #128871 both patch skills above the reviewer read budget; this PR caps autonomous skill size and restricts oversized skills to shrink-only rewrites.

## Evidence

- Live gateway (Linux, Telegram, `xai` provider) at `133ffe3`: manual experience review on a real foreground turn → `nothing` (usage: 0 uncached input, 13,902 cached, 36 output — the forked review hit the foreground prompt cache); manual collection review over the workspace → `succeeded`; the three oversized skills were rewritten under the cap (21,002 → 9,449; 11,882 → 7,735; 10,300 → 7,413 bytes, originals in `skill-workshop/collection-backups/`), the rest untouched, and the pre-PR "Read every current skill before reconciling" failure is gone. The next foreground turn's automatic experience review recorded `nothing` and `openclaw skills curator status` shows both outcomes. The apply recheck, MCP-runtime change (`26e821f`), and detached agent_end skip (`7e4a506`) landed after that run and are covered by the regression tests below.
- `pnpm test src/skills/workshop src/agents/tools/skill-workshop-tool src/gateway/server-methods/skills` plus `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.skills-policy.test.ts`, `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.tool-search-catalog-abort.test.ts`, `src/cli/skills-cli.curator.test.ts`, `src/agents/harness/tool-surface-bridge.test.ts` — green. New regression tests (`service.test.ts` agent-vs-operator apply on a user-authored skill and operator apply kept over a stale pending snapshot; `experience-review.apply.test.ts` no `cleanupBundleMcpOnRunEnd`; `attempt-phase-lifecycle.test.ts` no agent_end for a detached run; `code-mode-swarm.test.ts` swarm globals refused under the review allowlist) fail on the pre-fix code.
- Dependent sweep: 46 test files importing the touched modules — green.
- `oxfmt`, `scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` on changed files, `git diff --check` — clean.
- `pnpm tsgo && pnpm check:test-types` on Blacksmith Testbox — clean.
- Local ClawSweeper review (`gpt-5.6-terra`, high): `133ffe3` raised two findings (ownership recheck removed from the apply boundary; review retiring the shared session's MCP runtime), fixed in `26e821f`; `26e821f` raised one (detached review re-entering agent-end scheduling), fixed in `7e4a506`; `7e4a506` raised three: pending write racing an operator apply and Code Mode swarm globals bypassing the execution gate, both fixed in `e4b4322`; "prove detached review does not start configured MCP or LSP runtimes" is skipped as the cache-parity tradeoff stated above (LSP tool schemas come from the LSP runtime; the MCP runtime is session-owned and already warm). Maintainer decision on `e4b4322`: accepted — a detached review reuses the session MCP runtime and re-spawns configured per-attempt LSP servers exactly like a foreground turn; it still cannot execute them.
- Unrelated CI on `26e821f`/`7e4a506`: `check-lint-core-2` (`max-lines` in `src/gateway/server-methods/models-list-result.ts`, unused param in `models.test.ts`, both from #129332) and `checks-node-compact-small-8` (`doctor-auth.profile-health.test.ts`, Claude CLI auth from #129052) fail identically on `main` run 32857954734; `checks-node-compact-small-31` pins plugin SDK export counts (`4340` vs `4342`) that #129052 moved — this PR touches no `src/plugin-sdk` file. On `e4b4322` the failing set is the same twelve `checks-node-compact` shards that fail on `main` run 32857954734 (`large-5/12/13/14/15/18/22`, `small-8/14/20/21/26`) plus `small-31`; `check-lint-core-2` passes here. None are fixed here; #129357 carries the `main` fix.
- LOC (raw numstat): production +712 / −664 (net +48; the four review-fix commits after the live run add +76 / −26); tests + docs +1269 / −1238 (net +31).

* fix(cli-runner): drop stock watchdog defaults from CLI backend descriptors (#125045)

The claude-cli and gemini-cli backend descriptors spread
CLI_FRESH/RESUME_WATCHDOG_DEFAULTS into config.reliability.watchdog.
Those copies are byte-identical to the fallback pickWatchdogProfile
already uses, so shipping them only makes `configured` always truthy,
which permanently disables the promotion gate (!configured) and pins
resumed cron/explicit-timeout turns to the 180s resume no-output ceiling
instead of the 600s fresh ceiling.

Removing the blocks lets `configured` be undefined, restoring the
promotion gate. No user-config path is affected: reliability.watchdog
is not exposed in the config schema, the descriptor is the sole source,
and pickWatchdogProfile is the only runtime reader. The codex backend
never shipped the block, so this aligns the three backends.

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix: /models stops working after an unrelated config edit and never recovers (#128608)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix: /models stops working after an unrelated config edit and never recovers (#128608)

* fix: /models stops working after an unrelated config edit and never recovers

A config transaction whose reload plan is empty publishes the new runtime
config but never advances the prepared model owner's config stamp. Owners
are stamped with a hash of the whole config, so a key with no bearing on
models leaves every strict-policy catalog read rejected for the life of the
gateway process.

Advance the model-neutral config stamp in place on no-op publications
instead of rebuilding the prepared generation, which the planner has
already determined is unnecessary. Existing leases keep their immutable
snapshot, auth bindings carry onto the restamped snapshot, pending builds
restamp at commit, and read-only owners are untouched. Deferred startup
publication now resolves its config inside the serialized refresh so a
no-op commit landing mid-startup cannot publish an already-stale stamp.

Related: #128515

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(gateway): rebuild prepared owners from the committed runtime config

The no-op commit path resolves secrets and commits prepared.config, but the
rebuild that follows used the source-derived candidate. Where resolution
returns a different object -- secrets.providers.* edits, which are exactly
the changes that must rebuild rather than restamp -- the rebuilt owner
carries an identity no reader supplies, so every strict catalog read rejects
it and the failure this change removes reappears on its own fallback path.

Reuse the config the runtime-commit hook already receives, cleared per
transaction so a rebuild cannot inherit one committed by an earlier one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(gateway): cover the resolved-config auth rewarm

The ownership scenario returned the config secrets activation received, so a
rebuild against the source candidate looked correct. Let activation resolve
to a distinct object and assert by identity which config the rebuild used --
deep equality matches either object and proves nothing.

Fails without the committed-config selection, passes with it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(gateway): preserve prepared runtime options on auth rewarm

matched_commits.commit_message_snippet: fix(cli): normalize echoed binary tool outputs (#128699)
matched_commits.full_message:
fix(cli): normalize echoed binary tool outputs (#128699)

* fix(cli): image-heavy Claude CLI turns abort after about fifteen screenshots

The Claude CLI emits every image tool result twice in its stream-json
output: once inside `message.content[].tool_result.content[]` and once in
the `tool_use_result` field it echoes alongside the message. The
normalizer added in #119486 only walks the message copy, so the echoed
copy still counts against the 8 MiB per-turn raw-output budget and is
still retained in the live-turn line buffer.

Walk the whole parsed user record instead, so both copies are stubbed,
and cover the `tool_use_result.file.base64` shape the built-in image
read echoes. openclaw never reads `tool_use_result` (no references in
src), so nothing downstream changes.

[AI-assisted]

* fix(cli): make echoed-payload normalization stack-safe

Addresses the review finding on the recursive walker. The normalizer now
lives in its own module as one canonical entry point, walks the record
iteratively with an explicit stack, and falls back to raw accounting when
a record is too deeply nested for `JSON.stringify` to re-serialize.

Adds a 50,000-deep regression record, built as text because
`JSON.stringify` itself cannot serialize one that deep.
